rules.title: The freevxfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The freevxfs file system is a free implementation of the Veritas file system and is not used on typical Debian servers.
rules.impact: Disabling this reduces the risk of exploiting drivers and untrusted kernel code.

rules.title: The hfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: HFS is a legacy Apple file system. It is rarely needed on Linux servers and may contain unused code.
rules.impact: Disabling this reduces the potential attack surface in legacy modules.

rules.title: /tmp is a separate partition is configured
rules.explanation: The /tmp directory is world-writable and is used for temporary data storage by all users and some applications.
rules.impact: Creating /tmp as a separate filesystem allows the administrator to set additional mount options such as noexec, making /tmp useless to an attacker attempting to introduce executable code.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot attempt to create block or character special devices in /tmp.
rules.scope: Collection settings by the RHEL_8_scripts.sh script

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp filesystem is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /tmp.
rules.scope: Collection settings by the RHEL_8_scripts.sh script

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain executable files.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp file system is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot execute binary files from /tmp.
rules.scope: Collection settings by the RHEL_8_scripts.sh script

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var is configured
rules.explanation: The /var directory is used by daemons and other system services for temporary storage of dynamic data. Some directories created by these processes may be writable.
rules.impact: Because the /var directory can contain writable files and directories, there is a resource-exhaustion risk if it is not on a separate partition.
rules.scope: Collection settings by the RHEL_8_scripts.sh script

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var /tmp is configured
rules.explanation: The /var/tmp directory is a writable directory used for temporary storage by all users and some applications.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp directory is world-writable, there is a risk of resource exhaustion if it is not bound to a separate partition. In addition, giving /var/tmp its own file system allows the administrator to set the noexec option on the mount, making /var/tmp useless for an attacker installing executable code. It also prevents an attacker from creating a hard link to a system setuid program and waiting for it to be updated. Once the program is updated, the hard link is broken and the attacker has their own copy of the program. If a security vulnerability is found in the program, the attacker can continue to exploit the known flaw.
rules.scope: Collection settings by the RHEL_8_scripts.sh script

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /var/tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp file system is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot attempt to create block or character special devices in /var/tmp.
rules.scope: Collection settings by the RHEL_8_scripts.sh script

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var/tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp file system is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /var/tmp.
rules.scope: Collection settings by the RHEL_8_scripts.sh script

rules.title: The noexec parameter is set on the /var/tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain executable files.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp file system is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot execute files from /var/tmp.
rules.scope: Collection settings by the RHEL_8_scripts.sh script

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log is configured
rules.explanation: The /var/log directory is used by system services to store log data.
rules.impact: There are two important reasons to ensure that system logs are stored on a separate partition: protection against resource exhaustion (because logs can become quite large) and protection of audit data.
rules.scope: Collection settings by the RHEL_8_scripts.sh script

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log/audit is configured
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon stores log data in the /var/log/audit directory.
rules.impact: There are two important reasons to Ensure that data collected by auditd is stored on a separate partition: protection against resource exhaustion (because the audit.log file can become quite large) and protection of audit data. The audit daemon calculates how much free space remains and takes action based on the results. If other processes (for example, syslog) consume space on the same partition as auditd, it may not operate as intended.
rules.scope: Collection settings by the RHEL_8_scripts.sh script

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /home is configured
rules.explanation: The /home directory is used to support disk storage for local users.
rules.impact: If the system is intended to support local users, create a separate partition for the /home directory to protect against resource exhaustion and to limit the types of files that can be stored in /home.
rules.scope: Collection settings by the RHEL_8_scripts.sh script

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /home partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because user partitions are not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot attempt to create block or character special devices.
rules.scope: Collection settings by the RHEL_8_scripts.sh script

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /dev/shm is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating special devices on /dev/shm and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: Nosuid is set for /dev/shm in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nosuid prevents use of setuid/setgid on /dev/shm and reduces the risk of privilege elevation via shared memory.
rules.impact: If nosuid is missing, attacks using setuid binaries in shared memory are possible.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /dev/shm prevents execution of programs from shared memory, reducing the risk that users introduce and run malicious software from this location.

rules.title: SSH idle timeout interval is configured
rules.explanation: The ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax parameters control SSH session timeouts. When the ClientAliveInterval variable is set, ssh sessions that have no activity for the specified period of time are terminated. When the ClientAliveCountMax variable is set, sshd will send client alive messages at each ClientAliveInterval. When the number of consecutive client alive messages is sent without a response from the client, the ssh session is terminated.
rules.impact: The absence of a timeout value associated with a connection may allow an unauthorized user to access another user's ssh session (for example, a user leaves their computer and does not lock the screen). Setting a timeout value at least reduces this risk.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep clientaliveinterval

rules.title: SSH warning banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter specifies a file whose contents must be sent to the remote user before authentication is permitted. By default, no banner is displayed.
rules.impact: Banners are used to warn connecting users of the site-specific policy regarding connection. Presenting a warning message before the user's normal login can help in the prosecution of computer system violators.
rules.scope: sshd -T -C user=root -C host="$(hostname)" -C addr="$(grep $(hostname) /etc/hosts | awk '{print $1}')" | grep banner

rules.title: Default group for the root account GID 0
rules.explanation: The usermod command can be used to specify which group the root user belongs to. This affects permissions of files created by the root user.
rules.impact: Using GID 0 for the root account helps prevent accidental access to files with root permissions by unprivileged users.

rules.title: Permissions and ownership of bootloader configuration files are restricted is configured
rules.explanation: Access to bootloader configuration files must be restricted (root-only) to prevent unauthorized modification.
rules.impact: Incorrect permissions allow a local user to change boot parameters and potentially bypass security mechanisms.

rules.title: A password is set for the bootloader (GRUB) is configured
rules.explanation: A bootloader password prevents unauthorized changes to boot parameters and modification of the kernel/bootloader parameters with physical/local access.
rules.impact: The absence of a bootloader password allows an attacker to change kernel parameters (for example, disable AppArmor/SELinux) and bypass protections.

rules.title: A password is set for the bootloader (GRUB) is configured
rules.explanation: A bootloader password prevents unauthorized changes to boot parameters and modification of the kernel/bootloader parameters with physical/local access.
rules.impact: The absence of a bootloader password allows an attacker to change kernel parameters (for example, disable AppArmor/SELinux) and bypass protections.

rules.title: Kernel.yama.ptrace_scope is set to 1 or less is configured
rules.explanation: Restricting ptrace (ptrace_scope) prevents unsafe access between processes of different users.
rules.impact: Disabled or unrestricted ptrace may allow local users to interfere with other users' processes (a key privileged access risk).

rules.title: Core dumps are either disabled or that their permissions and storage location are secure (ulimit -c 0 or /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern) is configured
rules.explanation: Core dumps may contain sensitive data (passwords, keys). Restricting core file generation and permissions prevents disclosure of confidential information.
rules.impact: Unlimited core dumps increase the risk of secret data leakage when processes crash.

rules.title: SELinux is not disabled in the bootloader configuration is configured
rules.explanation: Configure SELinux to be enabled at boot and ensure that it has not been overridden by GRUB boot parameters.
rules.impact: SELinux must be enabled at boot in your GRUB configuration to ensure that the controls it provides will not be overridden.
rules.scope: The SELINUX parameter in /etc/selinux/config; the selinux and enforcing parameters in /etc/default/grub

rules.title: The SELinux state is enforcing is configured
rules.explanation: SELinux can be in one of three modes: disabled, permissive, or enforcing. Enforcing is the recommended default operating mode; in enforcing mode SELinux applies the loaded security policy to the entire system. Permissive - the system acts as if SELinux is applying the loaded security policy, including labeling objects and creating access-denial entries in the logs, but does not actually deny any operations. Although permissive mode is not recommended for production systems, it can be useful for SELinux policy development. Disabled is strongly not recommended; the system not only avoids enforcing the SELinux policy, but also avoids labeling any persistent objects such as files, which makes enabling SELinux in the future more difficult.
rules.impact: SELinux must be enabled at boot time to ensure that the controls it provides are continuously in effect.

rules.title: The SELinux policy is configured
rules.explanation: Configure SELinux to meet or exceed the default targeted policy, which confines only daemons and system software.
rules.impact: Security configuration requirements vary from site to site. Some sites may mandate a policy that is more stringent than the default policy, which is entirely acceptable. This item is intended to ensure that at least the default recommendations are met.

rules.title: SETroubleshoot is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The SETroubleshoot service notifies of SELinux denials through a convenient interface. The service provides important information about configuration errors, unauthorized intrusions, and other potential errors.
rules.impact: The SETroubleshoot service is an unnecessary daemon running on a server, especially if X Windows is disabled.

rules.title: The MCS translation service (mcstrans) is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The mcstransd daemon provides category label information to client processes that request information. Label translations are defined in /etc/selinux/targeted/setrans.conf.
rules.impact: Because this service is used infrequently, remove it to reduce the amount of potentially vulnerable code running on the system.

rules.title: SELinux is installed is configured
rules.explanation: SELinux provides mandatory access control.
rules.impact: Without a mandatory access control system in place, only the standard access control system will be available.

rules.title: The gdm3 package is not installed if a graphical interface is not required is configured
rules.explanation: If a graphical subsystem is not required on the server, it is recommended that GDM (GNOME Display Manager) be removed to reduce the attack surface.
rules.impact: Installing GDM on a server increases the number of services and potential vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The GDM configuration contains a correct banner (custom.conf or the corresponding profile) is configured
rules.explanation: GDM can display a banner at graphical session logon — it should be configured to match warning-banner policy.
rules.impact: The absence of a banner reduces user awareness and legal protection for graphical sessions.

rules.title: Disable-user-list=true is set in /etc/gdm3/greeter.dconf-defaults (or custom.conf) is configured
rules.explanation: The disable-user-list option prevents the user list from being displayed on the login screen, making it harder for an external observer to collect usernames.
rules.impact: A public user list facilitates login guessing and presents a social engineering risk.

rules.title: Automatic screen lock on idle is enabled in the GDM/GNOME configuration
rules.explanation: Automatic screen lock protects sessions from unauthorized access when the user is absent.
rules.impact: Lack of lockout increases the risk of access to open sessions.

rules.title: Lockout policies are applied globally and cannot be changed by users is configured
rules.explanation: Screen lock settings must not be user-overridable to prevent the security policy from being reset.
rules.impact: If users can disable the lock, protections against physical/local access become less effective.

rules.title: Automount policies in GDM/GNOME are disabled is configured
rules.explanation: Automounting removable media in a graphical environment increases the risk of malware spread and data leakage.
rules.impact: Automounting may result in automatic execution of or access to malicious files.

rules.title: Updates, patches, and additional security software are installed is configured
rules.explanation: Patches are periodically released for installed software either due to security flaws or to add additional functionality.
rules.impact: Newer patches may contain security improvements that will not be available after the latest full update. As a result, it is recommended to use the most recent software patches to take advantage of the newest functionality. As with any software installation, organizations need to determine whether a given update meets their requirements and verify compatibility and support of any additional software with the selected update version.

rules.title: Ypserv is disabled
rules.explanation: NIS is a legacy centralized authentication system.
rules.impact: NIS is vulnerable to password interception and network attacks.

rules.title: Chargen services are disabled (xinetd.d/chargen* or systemd-unit chargen*) is configured
rules.explanation: Chargen services (over TCP/UDP) are intended for testing but may be used for DoS attacks if enabled.
rules.impact: Enabled chargen services allow reflected DoS attacks.

rules.title: Daytime TCP/UDP services are disabled is configured
rules.explanation: The daytime service (ports 13/TCP and 13/UDP) returns the current system time in text form. This protocol is obsolete, does not require authentication, and must not be available on servers.
rules.impact: Legacy network services increase the attack surface.

rules.title: Ypbind is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The NIS client (ypbind) is also obsolete and should be removed unless compatibility is required.
rules.impact: NIS does not encrypt traffic and increases the risk of credential leakage.

rules.title: The rsh client is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The RSH client must be removed to prevent use of obsolete unencrypted protocols.
rules.impact: Using the rsh client may lead to password leakage and SSH policy bypass.

rules.title: The talk client is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: Talk client is a legacy program for network chat.
rules.impact: Legacy talk protocols do not encrypt data and are vulnerable to interception.

rules.title: The Telnet server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The telnet-server package contains the telnet daemon, which accepts connections from users of other systems via the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted. Using an unencrypted transmission medium may allow a user with access to network traffic analysis to steal credentials.

rules.title: Ldap-utils is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: If LDAP is not used in the infrastructure, its client packages should be removed to reduce the attack surface.
rules.impact: Unused LDAP increases the number of dependencies and vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The VSFTP server is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is a traditional and widely used standard tool for transferring files between a server and clients over a network, especially where authentication is not required (allowing anonymous users to connect to the server).
rules.impact: If there is no need to run the system as an FTP server, it is recommended that the package be removed to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The TFTP server is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) is a simple protocol for exchanging files between two TCP/IP computers. TFTP servers allow a TFTP client to connect to send and receive files.
rules.impact: TFTP has no built-in encryption, access control, or authentication. This allows an attacker to easily use TFTP to obtain access to files.

rules.title: The absence of IMAP and POP3 servers is configured
rules.explanation: IMAP and POP3 servers (dovecot-imapd, dovecot-pop3d) should not be installed unless required for operation.
rules.impact: These protocols are obsolete and vulnerable to attacks if not configured properly.

rules.title: Unused IMAP and POP3 server is not disabled is configured
rules.explanation: Dovecot is an open-source IMAP and POP3 server for Linux-based systems used by default.
rules.impact: If POP3 and/or IMAP servers are not provided on this system, it is recommended that the service be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: Samba is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The Samba daemon allows system administrators to configure their Linux systems to share filesystems and directories with Windows desktops. Samba will advertise filesystems and directories via the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. Windows desktop users will be able to mount these directories and filesystems as drive letters on their systems.
rules.impact: If there is no need to mount directories and file systems to Windows systems, this service can be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: Dnsmasq is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The dnsmasq DNS server must not be installed unless required for operations.
rules.impact: An unauthorized DNS server may be used for "DNS cache poisoning" attacks.

rules.title: Dnsmasq is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The dnsmasq DNS server must not be installed unless required for operations.
rules.impact: An unauthorized DNS server may be used for "DNS cache poisoning" attacks.

rules.title: The HTTP proxy server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: Squid is a standard proxy server used in many distributions and environments.
rules.impact: If a proxy server is not required, it is recommended to disable the squid proxy to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: NFS and RPC are not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The Network File System (NFS) is one of the earliest and most common file systems in the UNIX environment. It provides the ability for systems to mount file systems of other servers over the network.
rules.impact: If the system does not export NFS shares or act as an NFS client, it is recommended to disable these services to reduce the likelihood of a remote attack.

rules.title: Time synchronization is configured in /etc/ntp.conf or /etc/chrony.conf
rules.explanation: Time synchronization is important for audit and logging.
rules.impact: Inconsistent time causes audit errors and log desynchronization.

rules.title: Parameters for localhost and external sources are set in ntp.conf or chrony.conf is configured is restricted
rules.explanation: NTP restrict options limit access to the time service and prevent time spoofing.
rules.impact: Without restrict, an attacker can send malicious NTP responses.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0 and net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: Source-routed packets allow the sender to specify the path and bypass filters.
rules.impact: Accepting such packets enables routing and filtering bypass.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0 and net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: Source-routed packets allow the sender to specify the path and bypass filters.
rules.impact: Accepting such packets enables routing and filtering bypass.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0 and net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP Redirect messages can be used to redirect traffic to an attacker.
rules.impact: Accepting redirect packets allows traffic interception.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: If the system is not a router, it must not accept Router Advertisement (ICMPv6).
rules.impact: Accepting RA can change IPv6 routes and cause MITM.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: As with IPv4, disabling accept_redirects for IPv6 prevents route manipulation.
rules.impact: Accepting redirects can be used to bypass routes.

rules.title: Bogus ICMP responses are ignored is configured
rules.explanation: Some TCP/IP implementations generate responses to broadcast ICMP requests with incorrect error codes. Ignoring such responses protects against network scanning.
rules.impact: Without filtering spoofed ICMP replies, a server can be used to amplify attacks and network scanning. Incorrect ICMP messages may also disclose network topology information.

rules.title: ICMP broadcast requests are ignored is configured
rules.explanation: Responses to ICMP echo broadcast requests (Smurf attacks) can be used to amplify DDoS. Ignoring such requests prevents the server from participating in such attacks.
rules.impact: If the server responds to broadcast ICMP requests, an attacker can use it as an amplifier in a Smurf DDoS attack, generating traffic 500–1000 times the original.

rules.title: ICMP redirects are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP redirects can modify the kernel routing table. Accepting them from arbitrary hosts creates a vector for route poisoning attacks.
rules.impact: An attacker on the network can send spoofed ICMP redirects to change the server's traffic routing through their node. This is the basis of MITM attacks at the network layer.

rules.title: Secure ICMP redirects are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are accepted only from default gateways. Even this restriction does not guarantee protection, because a gateway may be compromised or spoofed.
rules.impact: Even secure ICMP redirects can be used by an attacker who has compromised the default gateway to alter server traffic routing for a MITM attack.

rules.title: Reverse path filtering is enabled
rules.explanation: Reverse Path Filtering (RPF) drops packets with a source IP address that is not reachable via the incoming interface. This is protection against IP spoofing.
rules.impact: Without RPF, an attacker can send packets with spoofed source IP addresses. This is used to bypass ACLs, implement blind TCP attacks, and spoof addresses in network attacks.

rules.title: Source-routed packets are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: IP source routing allows the sender to specify the packet path. This obsolete feature is used exclusively for attacks and must be disabled on all modern systems.
rules.impact: Source-routed packets allow an attacker to bypass firewalls and routing systems by forcing traffic through nodes they control for interception or modification.

rules.title: Suspicious packets are logged is configured
rules.explanation: Logging martian packets with impossible source addresses helps detect IP spoofing attempts and network anomalies. This is an important security monitoring capability.
rules.impact: Without logging of suspicious packets, IP-spoofing attacks and scans from forged addresses remain invisible. This substantially hinders intrusion detection and incident investigation.

rules.title: Audit logs are not deleted automatically is configured
rules.explanation: Configure the maximum audit log file size. Once the log reaches the maximum size, it is rotated and a new log file is started.
rules.impact: In high-security environments, the benefits of maintaining a long audit history outweigh the cost of storing audit history.

rules.title: The audit log storage size is configured
rules.explanation: The max_log_file_action parameter determines how to handle an audit log file that reaches the maximum size. The keep_logs value will rotate logs but never delete old logs.
rules.impact: It is important that an appropriate log file size is defined so that logs do not impact the system and audit data is not lost.

rules.title: The system is shut down when audit logs are full is configured
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon must be configured to halt the system when audit logs are full.
rules.impact: In a high-security context, the benefits of retaining a long audit history outweigh the cost of storing that history.

rules.title: The system is shut down when audit logs are full is configured
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon must be configured to halt the system when audit logs are full.
rules.impact: In a high-security context, the benefits of retaining a long audit history outweigh the cost of storing that history.

rules.title: The system is shut down when audit logs are full is configured
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon must be configured to halt the system when audit logs are full.
rules.impact: In a high-security context, the benefits of retaining a long audit history outweigh the cost of storing that history.

rules.title: The audit_backlog_limit parameter is configured
rules.explanation: The kernel-level audit subsystem uses a socket buffer queue to store audit events. Whenever a new audit event arrives, it is recorded and prepared for addition to this queue. The kernel boot parameter audit_backlog_limit=N, where N represents the number of messages, ensures that the queue cannot grow beyond a certain size. If an audit event is recorded that would cause the queue to exceed this limit, a failure occurs that is handled according to the system configuration.
rules.impact: If an audit event is recorded that causes the queue to grow beyond audit_backlog_limit, a failure occurs, audit records are lost, and potentially malicious activity may go unnoticed.

rules.title: The rsyslog service is enabled
rules.explanation: If the rsyslog service is not enabled, the system may default to using syslogd or log by other means.
rules.impact: If the rsyslog service is not enabled, the system may default to using syslogd or log by other means.

rules.title: Default rsyslog file permissions are configured
rules.explanation: Rsyslog will create log files that do not yet exist on the system. This setting controls which permissions are applied to those newly created files. The $FileCreateMode parameter specifies the file creation mode in which rsyslogd creates new files. If not specified, the value 0644 is used.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that log files have the correct permissions to enable archiving and protection of sensitive data.

rules.title: Rsyslog is configured to send logs to a remote log host
rules.explanation: The rsyslog utility supports sending collected logs to a running remote host or receiving messages from remote hosts, reducing administrative overhead.
rules.impact: Storing log data on a remote host protects log integrity from local attacks. If an attacker obtains root access on the local system, they can forge or delete log data stored locally.

rules.title: Password policies are set to minlen 14 and that character classes (upper, lower, digits, others) are enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/pwquality.conf file defines minimum password length and complexity.
rules.impact: Weak password requirements make passwords easy to guess.

rules.title: Deny 5 and unlock_time 900 are set in /etc/security/faillock.conf is configured
rules.explanation: The faillock mechanism locks an account after several failed logon attempts.
rules.impact: Without restrictions, password brute-force is possible.

rules.title: ENCRYPT_METHOD SHA512 in /etc/login.defs is configured
rules.explanation: The modern SHA-512 algorithm is resistant to brute-force attacks and should be used in /etc/login.defs and /etc/pam.d/ configurations.
rules.impact: Legacy MD5/DES methods provide weak password protection.

rules.title: SSH access is configured
rules.explanation: The AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers, or DenyGroups directives restrict which users are permitted SSH access. This implements the principle of least privilege for remote logon.
rules.impact: Without an explicit restriction, all system accounts, including service accounts, have SSH access. Compromise of any account provides a remote logon path and further persistence.

rules.title: The sshd banner is configured
rules.explanation: The SSH banner displays a warning before authentication.
rules.impact: A legal warning before logon may assist in legal proceedings.

rules.title: Sshd ciphers are configured
rules.explanation: Configure modern cryptographic algorithms for SSH.
rules.impact: Protection against outdated and insecure encryption algorithms.

rules.title: ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured
rules.explanation: Control SSH session inactivity timeout.
rules.impact: Preventing hanging sessions and conserving resources.

rules.title: DisableForwarding is enabled
rules.explanation: Prohibit port forwarding via SSH.
rules.impact: Reduce the risk of bypassing network restrictions.

rules.title: GSSAPIAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: Disable authentication via GSSAPI.
rules.impact: Simplifying configuration and removing unnecessary dependencies.

rules.title: Re-authentication on privilege elevation is not disabled globally is configured
rules.explanation: The global !authenticate flag in sudoers disables authentication for all users. This completely undermines the sudo security mechanism.
rules.impact: Globally disabling sudo authentication means that any user can obtain root privileges without entering a password. Capture of any user session immediately results in full system compromise.

rules.title: SSH X11 forwarding is disabled
rules.explanation: The X11Forwarding parameter provides the ability to tunnel X11 traffic over the connection to enable remote graphical sessions.
rules.impact: Disable X11 forwarding unless there is an operational requirement to use X11 applications directly. There is a small risk that remote X11 servers of users who logged in via SSH with X11 forwarding may be compromised by other users on the X11 server. Note that even if X11 forwarding is disabled, users can always set up their own forwarding servers.

rules.title: SSH MaxAuthTries is set to 4 or less is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxAuthTries parameter specifies the maximum number of authentication attempts permitted for a single connection. When the login failure counter reaches half of this value, error messages detailing the login failure are written to the system log file.
rules.impact: Setting MaxAuthTries to a low value minimizes the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. Although the recommended value is 4, set the number according to site policy.

rules.title: SSH IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: The IgnoreRhosts parameter specifies that .rhosts and .shosts files will not be used in RhostsRSAAuthentication or HostbasedAuthentication.
rules.impact: Setting this parameter requires users to enter a password when authenticating with ssh.

rules.title: SSH HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: The HostbasedAuthentication parameter specifies whether authentication via trusted hosts through user .rhosts or /etc/hosts.equiv, together with successful client host public-key authentication, is permitted. This option applies only to SSH protocol version 2.
rules.impact: Even if .rhosts files are ineffective when support is disabled in /etc/pam.conf, disabling the ability to use .rhosts files in SSH provides an additional layer of protection.

rules.title: Access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command allows a user to run a command or shell as another user. The program has been superseded by sudo, which provides more granular control over privileged access. Typically, the su command can be executed by any user. By uncommenting the pam_wheel.so statement in the /etc/pam.d/su file, the su command will allow only users in specified groups to execute su. This group should be empty to reinforce the use of sudo for privileged access.
rules.impact: Restricting use of su and using sudo instead allows system administrators to better control user privilege elevation for executing privileged commands. The sudo utility also provides a better logging and auditing mechanism because it can log every command executed via sudo, whereas su can only record that the user executed the su program.

rules.title: SSH PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitEmptyPasswords parameter specifies whether the SSH server permits authentication with empty password strings.
rules.impact: Denying remote shell access to accounts with an empty password reduces the likelihood of unauthorized access to the system.

rules.title: SSH PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitUserEnvironment parameter allows users to present environment options to the ssh daemon.
rules.impact: Allowing users to set environment variables via the SSH daemon can potentially allow users to bypass security measures (for example, setting an execution path in which ssh executes Trojan programs).

rules.title: SSH idle timeout interval is configured
rules.explanation: The ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax parameters control SSH session timeouts. When the ClientAliveInterval variable is set, ssh sessions that have no activity for the specified period of time are terminated. When the ClientAliveCountMax variable is set, sshd will send client alive messages at each ClientAliveInterval. When the number of consecutive client alive messages is sent without a response from the client, the ssh session is terminated.
rules.impact: The absence of a timeout value associated with a connection may allow an unauthorized user to access another user's ssh session (for example, a user leaves their computer and does not lock the screen). Setting a timeout value at least reduces this risk.

rules.title: SSH idle timeout interval is configured
rules.explanation: The ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax parameters control SSH session timeouts. When the ClientAliveInterval variable is set, ssh sessions that have no activity for the specified period of time are terminated. When the ClientAliveCountMax variable is set, sshd will send client alive messages at each ClientAliveInterval. When the number of consecutive client alive messages is sent without a response from the client, the ssh session is terminated.
rules.impact: The absence of a timeout value associated with a connection may allow an unauthorized user to access another user's ssh session (for example, a user leaves their computer and does not lock the screen). Setting a timeout value at least reduces this risk.

rules.title: SSH LoginGraceTime is set to one minute or less
rules.explanation: The LoginGraceTime parameter specifies the time allowed for successful authentication to the SSH server. The longer the grace period, the more unauthenticated connections may remain open. As with other session controls in this section, the grace period should be limited according to organizational constraints to ensure service availability for required access.
rules.impact: Setting a smaller value for LoginGraceTime minimizes the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. It also limits the number of concurrent unauthenticated connections.

rules.title: SSH warning banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter specifies a file whose contents must be sent to the remote user before authentication is permitted. By default, no banner is displayed.
rules.impact: Banners are used to warn connecting users of the site-specific policy regarding connection. Presenting a warning message before the user's normal login can help in the prosecution of computer system violators.

rules.title: All accounts have a non-empty password field in /etc/shadow is configured
rules.explanation: Each account must have a password hash set in /etc/shadow.
rules.impact: Passwordless accounts are a direct compromise threat.

rules.title: All accounts have a non-empty password field in /etc/shadow is configured
rules.explanation: Each account must have a password hash set in /etc/shadow.
rules.impact: Passwordless accounts are a direct compromise threat.

rules.title: System accounts (UID < 1000) have their shell set to /sbin/nologin or /bin/false is configured
rules.explanation: System accounts (UID<1000) must be locked or must not be able to log on.
rules.impact: Active system accounts create vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The root account primary group has GID 0 is configured
rules.explanation: Root must have GID 0 (root group) to ensure correct permissions and auditing.
rules.impact: An incorrect root group may grant access to unauthorized users.

rules.title: The default umask is set to 027 or more restrictive in /etc/login.defs and shell profiles is configured
rules.explanation: The umask parameter defines access permissions for newly created files and directories. The value 027 means: owner — full access, group — read/execute only, others — no access.
rules.impact: More permissive rights allow other users to read files.

rules.title: Password lifetime does not exceed 90 days
rules.explanation: The PASS_MIN_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to prevent users from changing their password until a minimum number of days have elapsed since the user's last password change.
rules.impact: The time during which an attacker can use compromised credentials, or successfully compromise credentials using an online brute-force attack, is limited by password age. Therefore, reducing the maximum password lifetime also reduces the attacker's window of opportunity.

rules.title: Password expiration warning period
rules.explanation: The PASS_WARN_AGE parameter in /etc/login.defs allows the administrator to notify users that their password will expire in a specified number of days.
rules.impact: Advance warning that a password is about to expire gives users time to consider a strong password.

rules.title: Password expiration warning period
rules.explanation: The PASS_WARN_AGE parameter in /etc/login.defs allows the administrator to notify users that their password will expire in a specified number of days.
rules.impact: Advance warning that a password is about to expire gives users time to consider a strong password.

rules.title: Lock inactive passwords
rules.explanation: User accounts that have been inactive for a specified period can be automatically disabled.
rules.impact: Inactive accounts pose a threat to system security because users do not log on to notice failed logon attempts or other anomalies.

rules.title: Lock inactive passwords
rules.explanation: User accounts that have been inactive for a specified period can be automatically disabled.
rules.impact: Inactive accounts pose a threat to system security because users do not log on to notice failed logon attempts or other anomalies.

rules.title: The password change date is not expired for all users is configured
rules.explanation: All users must have a password change date in the past.
rules.impact: If a user's recorded password change date has not yet occurred, they may bypass any configured password expiration.

rules.title: IgnoreRhosts is set to yes in /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: .rhosts and .shosts files must not be used for authentication.
rules.impact: Use of rhosts bypasses passwords.

rules.title: HostbasedAuthentication is set to no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: HostbasedAuthentication relies on trusted hosts and is not secure on open networks.
rules.impact: Using host-based authentication facilitates MITM attacks.

rules.title: The MaxAuthTries parameter in /etc/ssh/sshd_config is set to 4 or less is configured
rules.explanation: MaxAuthTries limits the number of failed SSH login attempts.
rules.impact: A large value allows brute-force attacks.

rules.title: The aide package is installed on the system is configured
rules.explanation: AIDE is used to monitor file system integrity and detect changes.
rules.impact: Absence of AIDE precludes change control capability.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/passwd is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd file contains user-account information that is used by many system utilities and therefore must be readable for those utilities to function.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that the /etc/passwd file is protected from unauthorized write access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or through malicious activity.

rules.title: /etc/group is owned by root:root and has permissions 644 is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/group defines user group membership.
rules.impact: Incorrect permissions allow users to change group membership.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/shadow is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow file is used to store user account information that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: If attackers can obtain read access to the /etc/shadow file, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed password to crack it. Other security information stored in the /etc/shadow file (for example, expiration) may also be useful for undermining user accounts.

rules.title: Permissions are 644 and the owner is root:root is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/passwd must be readable by all, but writable only by root.
rules.impact: Incorrect permissions allow modification of system credentials.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/group is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/group file contains the list of all valid groups defined on the system. The command below allows read/write access for root and read access for everyone else.
rules.impact: The /etc/group file should be protected from unauthorized modification by unprivileged users, but should be readable because this information is used by many unprivileged programs.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/shadow- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd- file contains backup user account information.
rules.impact: It is very important to ensure that the /etc/passwd- file is protected from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or through malicious activity.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/gshadow is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow file is used to store group information that is critical to the security of these accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: If attackers can obtain read access to /etc/gshadow, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed password to crack it.

rules.title: Regular filesystem integrity checking is configured
rules.explanation: Periodic file system integrity checking is required to detect changes in the file system.
rules.impact: Periodic file integrity checking allows the system administrator to regularly determine whether critical files have been modified in an unauthorized manner.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/passwd- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd- file contains backup user account information.
rules.impact: It is very important to ensure that the /etc/passwd- file is protected from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or through malicious activity.

rules.title: /etc/gshadow permissions are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/gshadow stores protected group data.
rules.impact: Access to gshadow discloses administrative group membership.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/shadow- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow-file is used to store backup information about user accounts that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as hashed passwords and other security information.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect /etc/shadow- from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed either accidentally or through malicious activity.

rules.title: /etc/shadow permissions are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shadow stores passwords and must be accessible only to root and the shadow group.
rules.impact: Access to shadow discloses password hashes.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/group- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/group file contains a backup list of all valid groups defined on the system.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect the /etc/group- file from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed either accidentally or through malicious activity.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/gshadow is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow file is used to store group information that is critical to the security of these accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: If attackers can obtain read access to /etc/gshadow, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed password to crack it.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/gshadow- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow file is used to store group information that is critical to the security of these accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: It is very important to ensure that the /etc/gshadow- file is protected from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or through malicious activity.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shells are configured correctly
rules.explanation: The /etc/shells file contains a list of valid login shells. Strict access permissions must be set on this file.
rules.impact: Restricting permissions prevents unauthorized modification of the list of allowed shells, which could lead to use of insecure shells.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/opasswd are configured correctly
rules.explanation: The /etc/opasswd file (if it exists) stores old password hashes. Access to this file must be restricted.
rules.impact: Protects older password hashes from unauthorized access, reducing the risk of brute-force attacks.

rules.title: No unused files or directories exist
rules.explanation: Sometimes when administrators remove users from the password file, they forget to remove all files belonging to those users from the system.
rules.impact: A new user who is assigned a user or group identifier of deleted users may eventually "own" those files and thus have greater access to the system than intended.

rules.title: Audit SUID executable files
rules.explanation: The file owner can set permissions to run the file with the owner's or group's permissions even if the user running the program is not the owner or a group member. The most common reason for an SUID program is to allow users to perform functions (such as changing their password) that require superuser privileges.
rules.impact: There are valid reasons for SUID programs, but it is important to identify and review such programs to ensure they are legitimate.
rules.scope: See section 6.1.13 in CentOS Linux 7 v4.0.0 (Audit/Remediation).

rules.title: Audit SGID executable files
rules.explanation: The file owner can set permissions to run the file with the owner's or group's permissions even if the user running the program is not the owner or a member of the group. The most common reason for using an SGID program is to allow users to perform functions (for example, changing their password) that require superuser privileges.
rules.impact: There are legitimate reasons for SGID programs, but it is important to identify and review such programs to ensure they are legitimate. Review the files returned by the audit action and check whether system binaries have an md5 checksum that differs from the one in the package. This indicates that the binary may have been replaced.

rules.title: No /etc/shadow entries have an empty password field is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shadow must not contain empty password fields.
rules.impact: An empty password field allows logon without authentication.

rules.title: There are no duplicate GID values in /etc/group is configured
rules.explanation: Each group must have a unique GID.
rules.impact: Duplicate GIDs cause incorrect privilege inheritance.

rules.title: OSSEC is installed is configured
rules.explanation: OSSEC (Open Source Host-based Intrusion Detection System) is a host-based intrusion detection system. It performs file integrity checking on your servers, logs various server activities, collects security events from your servers (and any others) and alerts on those events, produces various reports, and more.
rules.impact: By monitoring file system state, compromised files can be detected to prevent or limit the possibility of accidental or malicious misconfigurations or modified binaries.

rules.title: The syslog service is enabled
rules.explanation: If the syslog service is not enabled, logging will be disabled.
rules.impact: If the syslog service is not enabled, logging will be disabled.

rules.title: The syslog-ng service is enabled
rules.explanation: If the syslog-ng service is not enabled, the system may default to using syslogd or log by other means.
rules.impact: If the syslog-ng service is not enabled, the system may default to using syslogd or log by other means.

rules.title: Password creation requirements is configured
rules.explanation: The pam_pwquality.so module checks password strength. It verifies that the password is not a dictionary word, has a specified length, contains a set of character classes (for example, letters, digits, and so on), and more. pam_pwquality.so parameter definitions: try_first_pass - obtain the password from the previous stacked PAM module. If it is unavailable, prompt the user for a password; retry = 3 - allow 3 attempts before returning an error. The following parameters are set in /etc/security/pwquality.conf: minlen = 14 - the password must be at least 14 characters including a special character.
rules.impact: Strong passwords protect systems from brute-force attacks.

rules.title: Ypserv is disabled
rules.explanation: NIS is a legacy centralized authentication system.
rules.impact: NIS is vulnerable to password interception and network attacks.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0 and net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: IP forwarding (net.ipv4.ip_forward) should be disabled on systems that are not acting as routers.
rules.impact: Enabled forwarding allows cross-network traffic and MITM attacks.

rules.title: Auditd is installed is configured
rules.explanation: Auditd is the userspace component of the Linux audit system. It is responsible for writing audit records to disk.
rules.impact: Capturing system events provides system administrators with information that allows them to determine whether unauthorized access to their system is occurring.

rules.title: Auditd is enabled in grub
rules.explanation: Configure grub2 so that auditable processes can be audited even if they start before auditd starts.
rules.impact: Audit events must be captured for processes that start before audit so that potentially malicious activity cannot go unnoticed.

rules.title: Auditd rules for system date and time changes are configured
rules.explanation: Capture events when the system date and/or time were changed.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes to the system date and/or time may be an indication of malicious activity on the system.

rules.title: Events that change user or group information are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: Record events that affect changes to user or group information, including passwords and old passwords if they are used.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes in these files may indicate that the system has been compromised and that an unauthorized user is attempting to hide their activity or compromise additional accounts.

rules.title: Collection of events that modify discretionary access control permissions is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor changes to file permissions, attributes, owners, and groups. The parameters in this section monitor changes to system calls that affect file permissions and attributes. The chmod, fchmod, and fchmodat system calls affect permissions associated with a file. The chown, fchown, fchownat, and lchown system calls affect owner and group attributes on a file. setxattr, lsetxattr, fsetxattr (setting extended file attributes) and removexattr, lremovexattr, fremovexattr (removing extended file attributes) control extended file attributes. In all cases, an audit record will be written only for non-system user IDs (auid >=1000) and will ignore Daemon events (auid = 4294967295). All audit records will be tagged with the identifier "perm_mod".
rules.impact: Monitoring changes in file attributes can alert the system administrator to actions that may indicate attacker activity or a policy violation.

rules.title: Auditd rules for sudoers are configured
rules.explanation: Monitor scope changes for system administrators. If the system has been correctly configured to force system administrators to log in as themselves first and then use the sudo command to execute privileged commands, scope changes can be monitored. The /etc/sudoers file or files in /etc/sudoers.d will be written when the files or related attributes are changed. Audit records will be tagged with the identifier "scope".
rules.impact: Changes to /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d may indicate that an unauthorized change was made to the system administrator's scope of activity.

rules.title: Kernel module loading and unloading events are collected is configured
rules.explanation: Audit loading and unloading of kernel modules. The programs insmod (install a kernel module), rmmod (remove a kernel module), and modprobe (a more sophisticated program for loading and unloading modules, as well as some other functions) control module loading and unloading. The system calls init_module (load a module) and delete_module (delete a module) control module loading and unloading. Any execution of module load/unload programs and system calls generates an audit record with the identifier "modules".
rules.impact: Monitoring use of insmod, rmmod, and modprobe can provide system administrators evidence that an unauthorized user loaded or unloaded a kernel module, which may compromise system security. Monitoring the init_module and delete_module system calls will also record attempts by an unauthorized user to use another program to load and unload modules.

rules.title: Rsyslog is installed is configured
rules.explanation: Rsyslog software is recommended in environments where journald does not meet operational requirements.
rules.impact: Rsyslog security improvements, such as connection-oriented log transport (that is, TCP), the ability to log in database format, and encryption of log data in transit to a central log server, justify installing and configuring the package.

rules.title: The sudo package is installed on the system is configured
rules.explanation: The sudo package must be installed to control privilege elevation and to audit administrative commands.
rules.impact: Without sudo, root access is uncontrolled.

rules.title: Defaults use_pty is set in /etc/sudoers is configured
rules.explanation: The requiretty option enables auditing of sudo commands and protects against abuse via scripts.
rules.impact: Without a pty, sudo commands are harder to trace.

rules.title: Defaults logfile is defined in /etc/sudoers is configured
rules.explanation: Logging of sudo commands enables tracking of administrative actions.
rules.impact: Without logs it is impossible to investigate administrator actions.

rules.title: The pam_wheel module is enabled in /etc/pam.d/su to restrict use of su
rules.explanation: The su command must be allowed only for members of the wheel or sudo group.
rules.impact: Unrestricted su access increases the risk of unauthorized root logon.

rules.title: Permissions on SSH host public key files are configured
rules.explanation: An SSH public key is one of two files used in SSH public key authentication. In this authentication method, the public key is the key that can be used to verify digital signatures generated using the corresponding private key. Only the public key corresponding to the private key will be able to successfully authenticate.
rules.impact: If the host public key file is modified by an unauthorized user, the SSH service may be compromised.

rules.title: Users must enter a password to elevate privileges is configured
rules.explanation: NOPASSWD in sudoers disables the password requirement when executing privileged commands. Such entries must be excluded because they violate the principle of identity confirmation.
rules.impact: Without a password requirement, an attacker who obtains access to a user session (terminal hijacking, a compromised SSH key) immediately obtains full root privileges without an additional barrier.

rules.title: SSH PAM is enabled
rules.explanation: The UsePAM directive enables the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface. If set to "yes", this will enable PAM authentication using the ChallengeResponseAuthentication and PasswordAuthentication directives in addition to PAM account and session module processing for all authentication types.
rules.impact: If the usePAM parameter is set to yes, PAM correctly works with account and session types. This is important if you want to restrict access to services based on IP, time, or other account factors. In addition, you can ensure that users inherit certain environment variables at logon or deny access to the server.

rules.title: X11Forwarding no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: X11 forwarding transmits graphical sessions over SSH.
rules.impact: Enabled X11Forwarding allows attackers to use GUI tunneling.

rules.title: No duplicate usernames exist is configured
rules.explanation: Although useradd will not allow you to create a duplicate username, an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change the username.
rules.impact: If a user is assigned a duplicate username, they will create and have access to files with the first UID for that username in /etc/passwd. For example, if "test4" has UID 1000 and a subsequent "test4" entry has UID 2000, logging in as "test4" will use UID 1000. In effect, the UID is shared, which is a security issue.

rules.title: All GIDs specified in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group is configured
rules.explanation: Every group specified in /etc/passwd must exist in /etc/group.
rules.impact: A nonexistent group causes access control problems.

rules.title: Only the root account has UID 0 in /etc/passwd is configured
rules.explanation: Only root should have UID 0.
rules.impact: Multiple UID 0 accounts are a critical security error.

rules.title: The Audit service is enabled
rules.explanation: Enable the auditd daemon to record system events.
rules.impact: Collection of system events provides system administrators with information that allows them to determine whether unauthorized access to their system is occurring.

rules.title: Changes to files related to session events are audited is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor session initiation events. The parameters in this section track changes to files associated with session events.
rules.impact: Monitoring these files for changes can alert a system administrator to logons at unusual times, which may indicate attacker activity (that is, a user logging on at a time when they do not normally log on).

rules.title: Login and logout events are monitored is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor logon and logoff events.
rules.impact: Monitoring logon/logoff events can provide the system administrator with information related to attacks against user logon.

rules.title: System calls related to deleting or renaming files and file attributes are audited is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor use of system calls related to deleting or renaming files and file attributes.
rules.impact: Tracking these calls from unprivileged users can provide the system administrator with evidence that improper deletion of files and file attributes associated with protected files is occurring. Although this audit option will capture all events, system administrators will want to look for specific privileged files that are deleted or modified.

rules.title: The nodev option is set for the /var partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because /var is not intended to support devices, this option prevents the creation of block or character devices on this partition.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set for the /var partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid option prohibits use of setuid files in the file system.
rules.impact: Because /var is intended for variable files (for example, logs), this option prevents creation of potentially dangerous executables with elevated privileges.

rules.title: The nodev option is set for the /var/log partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev option prevents the use of special devices on the filesystem.
rules.impact: The /var/log partition is intended only for log storage, so device files are not required there and may be dangerous.

rules.title: The noexec option is set for the /var/log partition is configured
rules.explanation: The noexec option prevents execution of programs on this partition.
rules.impact: Because /var/log contains only logs, executable files are not needed there and their presence could be used for attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set for the /var/log partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid option disables the use of setuid files.
rules.impact: Logs must not contain executable files with elevated privileges, as this may lead to privilege escalation.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /var/log/audit partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev option prevents device creation on the partition.
rules.impact: Audit logs should not contain devices, as this can be used to bypass access control.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /var/log/audit partition is configured
rules.explanation: The noexec option prohibits code execution on this partition.
rules.impact: Audit logs must not contain executable files, to prevent execution of malicious code.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var/log/audit partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid option disables setuid files on the partition.
rules.impact: Audit logs must not contain files with elevated privileges, as this may lead to privilege escalation.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set for the /home partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid option prohibits the use of setuid files in user home directories.
rules.impact: Users must not be able to create executable files with elevated privileges in their home directories.

rules.title: Gpgcheck is enabled globally
rules.explanation: The gpgcheck parameter, located in the main section of /etc/yum.conf and in individual /etc/yum/repos.d/*.repo files, determines whether the RPM package signature is verified before installation.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that the RPM package signature is always verified before installation to guarantee that the software is obtained from a trusted source.

rules.title: Default user umask value
rules.explanation: The user file-creation mode mask (umask) is used to determine the access permissions of newly created directories and files. In Linux, the default permissions for any newly created directory are 0777 (rwxrwxrwx), and for any newly created file are 0666 (rw-rw-rw-). Umask modifies the default Linux permissions by restricting (masking) those permissions. Users who want their files and directories to be readable by other users by default may choose a different default umask by inserting a umask command into the standard shell configuration files (.profile, .bashrc, etc.) in their home directories.
rules.impact: Setting a secure default umask ensures that users make a conscious choice regarding file access permissions. A permissive umask value can result in directories or files with excessive permissions that can be read and/or written by unauthorized users.

rules.title: ASLR is enabled (kernel.randomize_va_space = 2)
rules.explanation: ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization) makes it harder to predict stack/library locations, which complicates exploitation of buffer overflow vulnerabilities.
rules.impact: Disabled ASLR significantly simplifies successful exploitation of vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The SELinux state is enforcing is configured
rules.explanation: SELinux can be in one of three modes: disabled, permissive, or enforcing. Enforcing is the recommended default operating mode; in enforcing mode SELinux applies the loaded security policy to the entire system. Permissive - the system acts as if SELinux is applying the loaded security policy, including labeling objects and creating access-denial entries in the logs, but does not actually deny any operations. Although permissive mode is not recommended for production systems, it can be useful for SELinux policy development. Disabled is strongly not recommended; the system not only avoids enforcing the SELinux policy, but also avoids labeling any persistent objects such as files, which makes enabling SELinux in the future more difficult.
rules.impact: SELinux must be enabled at boot time to ensure that the controls it provides are continuously in effect.

rules.title: Unrestricted services do not exist is configured
rules.explanation: Unconfined processes run in unconfined domains.
rules.impact: Unconfined processes are subject to SELinux policy rules, but there are policy rules that allow processes running in unconfined domains nearly all access. Processes running in unconfined domains fall back to using DAC rules exclusively. If an unconfined process is compromised, SELinux does not prevent an attacker from accessing system resources and data, but DAC rules are still applied. SELinux is a security enhancement on top of DAC rules, not a replacement for them.

rules.title: Remove GNOME Display Manager (GDM)
rules.explanation: GDM is the graphical login manager for GNOME.
rules.impact: If GDM is not used, removing it reduces the likelihood of attack.

rules.title: The disable-user-list parameter in GDM is configured
rules.explanation: GNOME Display Manager (GDM) handles graphical logon on GNOME-based systems. The disable-user-list setting controls display of the user list on the logon screen. Using lock mode in dconf, you can prevent users from changing certain settings.
rules.impact: Displaying the user list eliminates half of the username/password equation that an unauthorized person would need to log on. Without locking system settings, user settings take precedence over system settings.

rules.title: XDMCP is disabled
rules.explanation: XDCMP allows remote control of X11 sessions.
rules.impact: Disabling this prevents potential remote access attacks.

rules.title: The system-wide cryptographic policy is not set to legacy is configured
rules.explanation: System-wide crypto policies followed by core cryptography components allow algorithms to be consistently deprecated and disabled across the entire system.
rules.impact: If the system-wide Legacy crypto policy is selected, it includes support for TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and SSH2 or later. DSA, 3DES, and RC4 algorithms are allowed, while RSA and Diffie-Hellman parameters are accepted if they are greater than 1023 bits. These legacy protocols and algorithms can make the system vulnerable to attacks, including those listed in RFC 7457.

rules.title: Telnet is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The Telnet client may be used to access insecure server services.
rules.impact: Telnet transmits logins and passwords in cleartext.

rules.title: The VSFTP server is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is a traditional and widely used standard tool for transferring files between a server and clients over a network, especially where authentication is not required (allowing anonymous users to connect to the server).
rules.impact: If there is no need to run the system as an FTP server, it is recommended that the package be removed to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The FTP server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: File Transfer Protocol (FTP) allows networked computers to transfer files between a server and clients over a network where authentication is absent (disallow anonymous user connections to the server).
rules.impact: FTP does not protect the confidentiality of data or credentials. It is recommended to use sftp if file transfer is required. If there is no need to run the system as an FTP server (for example, to allow anonymous downloads), it is recommended that the service be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: Rpcbind is not installed or rpcbind services are masked is configured
rules.explanation: The rpcbind utility maps RPC services to the ports they listen on. RPC processes notify rpcbind at startup, registering the ports they listen on and the RPC program numbers they expect to serve. A client system then contacts rpcbind on the server with a specific RPC program number. The rpcbind service redirects the client to the correct port number so it can contact the requested service. Portmapper is an RPC service that always listens on TCP and UDP 111 and is used to map other RPC services (such as nfs, nlockmgr, quotad, mountd, and so on) to the corresponding port number on the server. When a remote host makes an RPC call to this server, it first consults portmap to determine where the RPC server is listening.
rules.impact: A small request (~82 bytes over UDP) sent to Portmapper generates a large response (amplification of 7x to 28x), making it a suitable tool for DDoS attacks. If rpcbind is not required, it is recommended that the rpcbind package be removed to reduce the system's attack surface.

rules.title: Chrony is not run as the root user is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/sysconfig/chronyd file allows configuration of parameters for chrony, including the user under which chrony runs. By default this is the chrony user.
rules.impact: Services must not be configured to run as the root user.

rules.title: Actions of another user are always logged is configured
rules.explanation: Sudo provides users with temporary elevated privileges to perform operations as the superuser or another user.
rules.impact: Creating an audit log of users with temporarily elevated privileges and the operations they performed is essential for reporting. Administrators may want to correlate events recorded in the audit trail with entries recorded in the sudo log file to verify that unauthorized commands were not executed.

rules.title: Events that modify the sudo log file are collected is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor the sudo log file. If the system has been correctly configured to disable use of the su command and to require all administrators to log in first and then use sudo to execute privileged commands, all administrator commands will be recorded in /var/log/sudo.log. Each time a command is executed, an audit event will be generated because /var/log/sudo.log will be opened for writing, and the executed administrative command will be written to the log.
rules.impact: Changes to /var/log/sudo.log indicate that an administrator executed a command or that the log file itself was tampered with. Administrators may want to correlate events recorded in the audit log with entries in /var/log/sudo.log to verify that unauthorized commands were not executed.

rules.title: Auditd rules for programs with setuid and/or setgid are configured
rules.explanation: Monitor privileged programs that have the setuid and/or setgid bit set on execution to determine whether unprivileged users are executing these commands.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes to the system date and/or time may be an indication of malicious activity on the system.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chcon command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful use of the chcon command.
rules.impact: Without generating audit records that relate to the organization's security and mission requirements, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate incident-related events or determine those responsible.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the setfacl command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful or unsuccessful use of the setfacl command.
rules.impact: Without generating audit records that relate to the organization's security and mission requirements, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate incident-related events or determine those responsible.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chacl command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful or unsuccessful use of the chacl command.
rules.impact: Without generating audit records that relate to the organization's security and mission requirements, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate incident-related events or determine those responsible.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the usermod command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful use of the usermod command.
rules.impact: Without generating audit records that relate to the organization's security and mission requirements, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate incident-related events or determine those responsible.

rules.title: The audit configuration is immutable is configured
rules.explanation: Configure system audit so that audit rules cannot be changed using auditctl. Setting the "-e 2" flag forces audit into immutable mode. Audit changes can be made only when the system is rebooted.
rules.impact: In immutable mode, unauthorized users cannot make changes to the audit system to potentially conceal malicious activity and then restore the audit rules. Users are likely to notice a system reboot, and this may alert administrators to an attempt to make unauthorized audit changes.

rules.title: The running configuration and the on-disk configuration are the same is configured
rules.explanation: The audit system has both on-disk and current configuration. These configuration parameters may differ.
rules.impact: Differences between the currently running configuration and what is on disk can cause unexpected problems or create a false impression of compliance.

rules.title: Root can log in only via console or SSH with a key is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/securetty file must contain only valid terminals for root.
rules.impact: Unauthorized root access increases the escalation risk.

rules.title: The system-wide cryptographic policy is not overridden is configured
